transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-27 14:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Linnea (Redwood SE), Marcus (Redwood Product), Aisha (CoralGrid), Ben (CoralGrid), Ravi (CoralGrid CTO), Maya (CoralGrid security)

Auto-summary: quick demo of hosted chat streaming, walk-through of common param tradeoffs and live console to show latency/cost traces. Covered retry patterns and fallback to smaller variants. Security questions about audit logs and KMS.

00:00 Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Samir from Redwood inference, and with me is linnea our se and marcus from product. how's everyone doing?
00:06 Aisha: good, thanks. excited to see the hosted api flow; we're evaluating for customer chat assistants and internal search snippets.
00:14 Samir: great. quick agenda: we'll do a short live run of the chat endpoint, show streaming behavior, go into the console to look at traces and cost breakdowns, then show retry/backoff patterns and our optimize suggestions for cost/latency tradeoffs. save q's for the end or interrupt anytime.
00:27 Ben: quick note — we run on GKE and want to pin to a VPC egress pattern, so we'll ask about network later.
00:33 Linnea: noted. we'll cover private deployment notes and KMS in the security section.
00:36 Samir: ok starting with a simple chat demo. i'm going to post a request with a system prompt, user history, and stream it back. you should see tokens come in as chunks.
00:48 Samir: (typing) calling conversations.create with model: redwood-open-1, temperature: 0.2, top_p: 0.9, max_tokens: 256, stream: true.
01:05 Aisha: oh neat, already getting partial tokens — latency looks good from here.
01:10 Linnea: one note: streaming granularity depends on model and batching; small tokens flush quicker but can increase RPC overhead. we tune threshold vs latency.
01:24 Samir: and if you look at the console — i'll switch over — we can see the request entry, per-route latency, token count, and cost estimate in near real time.
01:36 Marcus: also showing the token-level cost breakdown per client token vs model tokens, that helps correlate spikes.
01:45 Maya: on the console, do you keep raw transcripts? retention? we need to know about PII and audit logs.
01:53 Samir: yes so hosted keeps short-term logs for debugging; for regulated setups we recommend either private deployment or configure retention via the console. you'll see audit events and SSO access logs. we'll share the SOC2 doc after.
02:07 Aisha: could you talk through retries? we want deterministic behavior for our idempotent calls.
02:12 Linnea: sure. there are two axes: client-side idempotency/duplication and server-side retry/backoff. for streaming, we recommend using request ids and a short exponential backoff with jitter. if a stream disconnects mid-response we send a final status and you can either re-ask with the same id and resume from last token (client re-assembly), or fall back to a synchronous generation call to get the full answer.
02:38 Ben: do you provide builtin resume tokens?
02:41 Linnea: we don't have a seamless resume token across every model yet; it's on the roadmap. current pattern is to cache prefix (KV cache) on the client and rehydrate, or keep small final checkpoints. we do provide automatic KV cache at the runtime layer for repeated prompts within the same conversation which saves cost. note that's runtime kv not exposed as raw offsets.
03:04 Ravi: latency vs cost question — we need sub 250ms p95 for short responses. can you hit that on hosted?
03:12 Marcus: depends on model and tokens. for short completions with redwood-open-1 small variants, yes in many regions we hit ~150ms p95 for <40 tokens. throughput and batching will change that; console lets you pick a route policy to prioritize latency over throughput.
03:29 Aisha: i saw an Optimize suggestion earlier in the console about quantization and batching. can you show that?
03:34 Samir: switching to Optimize tab — here the Recommend view surfaces model variants and quantization suggestions based on your workload. for example, if your token lengths are short and predictable, Optimize suggests a 4-bit quantized variant and more aggressive batching to reduce unit cost.
03:51 Linnea: a caveat: more batching reduces unit cost but increases tail latency. Optimize gives an expected p95 impact so you can decide the tradeoff.
04:06 Ben: how do rollouts work if we pin versions? we need deterministic model versions across environments.
04:12 Samir: you can pin model versions per route in the console and define canary percentages. if a variant fails, the routing layer falls back to the compatible variant — weight-based or fixed fallback.
04:24 Aisha: back to retries — what's the idempotency token header name?
04:28 Linnea: we suggest X-Request-Id for customer idempotency mapping; we also return a request_status field in the stream completion event. use exponential backoff with 200ms base and cap at ~2s for streaming reconnects.
04:43 Ravi: any gotchas with large contexts? we sometimes send 8k tokens including docs.
04:48 Linnea: for large contexts use KV cache and chunking. the runtime uses attention optimizations and can select longer-sequence kernels, but cost rises linearly with context. Optimize will flag high-context calls and recommend caching or embedding strategies.
05:06 Samir: we'll demo a reconnect scenario now. i'm going to intentionally drop the network stream.
05:12 Samir: (simulated) stream disconnect at 05:12 — client reconnect attempt with same X-Request-Id and small resume logic — you see the client receives a partial "stream interrupted" event in the console.
05:34 Aisha: so best practise is to persist last token index on the client and decide resume vs fallback?
05:40 Linnea: yep. and for stateful conversations we strongly suggest keeping a conversation id and storing conversation history server-side so you can rehydrate and avoid hallucination on resume.
05:51 Ben: can you demonstrate the console's trace for that failed request?
05:56 Samir: switching to traces — here's the failed stream entry, shows stage: queued -> dispatched -> partial -> interrupted. there's a stack of retries and eventual fallback to a smaller model variant we configured as a safe fallback.
06:13 Marcus: that fallback is policy-driven; you can choose fallback to a cheaper quantized variant or to a dedicated reserved node if you have capacity.
06:23 Maya: security: how are keys rotated and where is KMS used?
06:27 Samir: we integrate with customer KMS for private deployments and offer managed keys for hosted. rotation is monthly by default for managed keys; for private we support customer-managed keys and HSM-backed rotation. we'll send the KMS integration spec.
06:40 Maya: audit logs for message content — is it stored encrypted at rest?
06:44 Samir: yes, encrypted at rest; you can opt-out of log retention of content, keep only metadata for debugging, and we can also give a private deployment for complete control.
06:56 Aisha: ok can you show a param tuning example — like moving temperature and seeing output differences live?
07:01 Linnea: sure, let's run two quick examples side-by-side: one with temperature 0.0 deterministic, and one with 0.8 more creative.
07:12 Samir: starting run A temp=0.0 max_tokens=80, stream=true.
07:22 Samir: run B temp=0.8 max_tokens=80, stream=true.
07:33 Aisha: i can already see run B is producing synonyms and more varied phrasing. run A is concise. this is exactly the behavior we wanted to compare.
07:42 Linnea: note top_p interacts with temperature; if you set top_p=0.5 you will cap sampling to a smaller cumulative prob mass which can reduce risk of rare tokens.
07:53 Ben: do you recommend using top_p over temperature?
07:56 Linnea: prefer temperature for general randomness control; use top_p when you want a hard cap on token distribution. both are fine but watch interplay. Optimize can surface a recommended pair based on your evaluation prompts.
08:10 Marcus: small demo of console Evaluate: we uploaded a few prompt/expected pairs and Optimize scored candidate model variants for MRR and latency. here's a chart — redwood-open-1-quant had 12% cost reduction with similar MRR.
08:29 Aisha: nice — can we run our own test set during the pilot?
08:33 Samir: yes, we'll provision a sandbox project and share a notebook so you can push your evals; Optimize will run the regression checks and alert if quality regresses.
08:44 Linnea: moving to retry strategies — i'll show sample client pseudocode. (reads) start call; set idempotency header; on error if status is transient (5xx, 429) retry with exp backoff; for stream disconnects try one reconnect, then fallback to a synchronous call or smaller model. avoid blind retries for non-idempotent writes.
09:12 Ben: do you surface 429 throttle headers?
09:15 Linnea: yes rate-limit headers include X-RateLimit-Remaining and a Retry-After in seconds; console also surfaces per-route quota usage so you can preemptively tune.
09:26 Samir: quick tangent — billing model: tokens in and tokens out billed; streaming doesn't change billing semantics but helps perceived latency. Optimize can estimate cost-per-conversation.
09:40 Aisha: how does dedicated differ cost/latency wise?
09:44 Marcus: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools — more predictable p95 and isolation from noisy neighbors; hosted has multi-tenant efficiencies and faster onboarding. if you need strict SLA, Dedicated or Private is recommended.
09:58 Ravi: our timeline: want to pick a vendor within 6 weeks and run a 1-week pilot. what's the minimum reserved for a pilot?
10:05 Samir: for Dedicated pilots we often do a small reserved slot for a week; for Hosted you can start a sandbox project immediately with credit. we'll send a sample pilot quote.
10:14 Maya: data residency — can we keep data in eu region?
10:18 Samir: yes, you can select region and we have EU regions for hosted; for strict residency and compliance Private is the option.
10:26 Linnea: going to show a live failure-mode lab we run with customers — different types of disconnects and best responses. first: stream chunk delay where tokens arrive slowly; second: abrupt socket close; third: transient 5xx.
10:41 Samir: demo 1: slow tokens — we show client-side spinner and a partial confidence metric; console flags long-tail latency and suggests switching to a lower batch size to reduce token flush latency.
10:56 Samir: demo 2: socket close — we show reconnect and resume logic; console marks the request with interrupted=true.
11:10 Linnea: demo 3: 5xx — policy triggers fallback to quantized variant and sends alerting to ops channel.
11:20 Ben: question — can we implement region failover automatically?
11:24 Marcus: yes policy routing supports region fallback; you can route primary EU then fallback to US with notice. some customers avoid cross-border by using Private.
11:33 Aisha: last technical q — are embeddings used for context fallback?
11:37 Linnea: yes, embedding + retrieval is a common pattern: store docs as embeddings and fetch top-k for context, reduces long context costs. Optimize flags when you should switch from full context to retrieval.
11:50 Samir: wrapping up with a quick recap of recommended next steps: set up sandbox project, run your eval set in Optimize, we'll send security+KMS doc and a pilot quote.
12:01 Ravi: sounds good. one ask — please include a sample of console traces for a 250ms p95 run so we can demonstrate to stakeholders.
12:09 Samir: noted, will include.
12:12 Maya: will we get a contact for SSO/SAML configuration?
12:15 Samir: yes, i'll CC our infra-ops person; we'll send the SAML guide and SSO checklist.
12:22 Aisha: thanks — the live demo was helpful, and the Optimize auto-suggests look promising.
12:28 Samir: any other questions? (silence) ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the items we listed. expect docs and quote by end of week.
12:39 End of recording.
